title: Four Worlds Built Alike
question: What do the Solar System's inner planets have in common?
hook: Four very different worlds hide the same anatomy.
idea: Terrestrial planets are solid-surfaced worlds of rock and metal, with a metal core, a silicate mantle and an atmosphere made on the planet itself.

beats.prompt: You could slice an inner planet like Mars or Venus in half. What would you find?

choices.label: A metal core, mostly iron, inside a silicate mantle
A solid ball of ice all the way through
choices.feedback: Ice-and-rock worlds exist, but they lie farther out; inner planets are built of rock and metal.

choices.label: A hollow centre under a thin rocky shell
choices.feedback: Nothing suggests hollow worlds; each has a central metallic core.

beats.explain: All terrestrial planets in the Solar System share a central metallic core, mostly iron, with a surrounding silicate mantle.

beats.prompt: match each kind of world to what it is made of
beats.explain: The classes differ in their materials: rock and metal, ice and rock, or hydrogen, helium and water.

beats.prompt: sort each source of air into the kind of atmosphere it makes
items: Gas captured from the early solar nebula
beats.explain: Terrestrial planets make their air from volcanoes or comet debris, while giant planets captured theirs from the solar nebula.

beats.prompt: one step in this reasoning is wrong; which?
steps: Terrestrial planets have a solid surface.
Larger gaseous planets are mostly hydrogen, helium and water.
So a terrestrial planet must be mostly hydrogen and helium.
So the two kinds differ in what they are made of.
beats.explain: Terrestrial planets are silicate, rock or metal; hydrogen and helium make up the larger gaseous planets.
